The Circassian–Nogai wars were a series of military conflicts between the Circassian tribes, the Abazins, and the Nogai Horde (often allied with the Crimean Khanate) from the 16th to the 18th centuries. The Nogais, who were subjects of the Crimean Khanate, frequently raided Circassian and Abazin lands. The Circassians and Abazins responded with their own raids. The wars ended with a Circassian victory. The Nogais were expelled from Circassian and Abazin lands.
List of raids and battles
Beslan the Fat's Astrakhan campaign
In 1532, Ak-Kubek fled to Kabardia and appealed to Beslan for assistance. Beslan gathered a strong army and marched on Astrakhan with the aim of capturing the city and restoring Ak-Kubek to the throne. The forces were joined by the Principality of Hatuqay, led by a prince nicknamed "the Pale", and probably also by the Chemguy, who traditionally acted in alliance with them. During the campaign the Kabardian warrior Andemirkan reportedly distinguished himself by being the first to cross the Volga and by killing the opposing commander during the capture of Astrakhan. In the ensuing battle the Adyghe forces captured the city, killing Kasim and many of his supporters. This event was also reflected in Russian chronicles:
"Having arrived at Aztorakan, the Cherkasy, unknown to anyone, took Astrakhan, killed the tsar and princes, plundered their possessions, and departed. And Tsarevich Ak-Kubek began to rule in Astrakhan."
Ghazi ibn Urak's campaign in Kabardia (1576)
In 1576, the forces of the Lesser Nogai bey Ghazi ibn Urak were defeated by the Kabardians led by Temryukites and Sholokh Tepsaruqo. Nogai forces entered Kabardia and killed many, but they were briefly defeated by the Kabardians on their return. In addition to Ghazi ibn Urak, two of his brothers and several of his sons, as well as Iman-Girey and Chebar-Murza were murdered by the Kabardian forces during one of the battles. Pshiapshoqo Qeytuqo fought on the side of the Nogais and the Crimeans, pursuing a pro-Crimean policy.
Kabardian-Nogai war (1587)
In 1587, the Pyatigorsk Circassians drove away horses from the Nogai leader Ekshisat. The Don Cossacks then attacked him, plundered his uluses, and captured his married daughter and her children.
Kabardian–Nogai war (1613–1619)
In 1613, the Nogai ruler Biy Ishterek moved into Kabardian lands. The Kabardians attacked him. He suffered a heavy defeat and was forced to relocate to the steppes between the Terek and Astrakhan. Between 1616 and 1619, Aledjuqo Shodjenuqo led a coalition of Kabardians, Western Circassians, Kumyks, and Chechens against the Great Nogais. The Great Nogais were forced to move from the right bank of the Volga to the left bank.
Kabarian–Nogai war (1630)
In 1630, Sholokh Sunchaleyevich Cherkassky led incursions into Nogai settlements, devastating the lands, stealing livestock, and killing many nomadic Nogai forces In the same year, Mutsal Cherkassky with his regiment of 1,200 Kabardians and Terek Cossacks raided Nogai uluses near Azov. Avoiding the heavily fortified Azov, they destroyed the large Nogai ulus of Murza Shantemir on the Yeya River. The victors captured up to 7,000 prisoners, 6,000 cows and 2,000 sheep.
Raid on the Kaziev Nogais (1636)
In 1636, a combined force under Prince S. Volkonsky, including 200 streletsys, Circassian cavalry, Chechens, other peoples from the Terek basin, as well as Terek and Greben Cossacks, set out on a campaign against the Nogai ulus of Kaziyev. S. Volkonsky also had an agreement with the Don Cossacks, however they couldn't arrive at time. Therefore, without waiting for the Don Cossacks, the joint forces led by Volkonsky attacked the Nogais, after a fierce battle, the Nogais were defeated and subsequently devastated. The allied forces expanded deeper into Nogai territory —as far as Astrakhan—, then retreated with success.
Kasbulat Cherkassky's campaign (1672)
In 1672, Prince Kasbulat Cherkassky, supported by Kalmyk Khan Ayuka and the Terek Cossacks, devastated the lands of his pro-Crimean enemies. The Nogais were among the victims. In 1672, the Kalmyk taisha Ayuka destroyed the Lesser Nogai Horde (Kaziyev ulus). In response, Nogai murzas killed Kasbulat's younger brother Kantemir. Kasbulat then called on Ayuka's Kalmyks and, together with the Terek Cossacks, devastated the lands of his enemy, the Nogai Murza Karaksai, crushed his uluses, stealing livestock and killing many.
Nogai-Crimean raids on Circassia (1710)
In 1710, Crimean Tatars and Nogai forces led incursions into Western Circassia and Kabardia to collect booty. Tribute was collected and large numbers of livestock and horses were stolen, Nogai's and Crimeans retreated with success.
Chemguy-Nogai conflicts
Oral traditions recorded by Khan-Giray describe a period of intense warfare between the Chemguy Circassians and the Nogais during the Nogai migrations south of the Volga. During this conflict, a major battle resulted in the destruction of an elite Chemguy force led by Prince Karbech Boletuqo against the Nogais. The death of Karbech, along with other prominent warriors, were preserved in heroic songs. Songs about the event historically considered "cursed" and were not to be sung during military expeditions. By 1735, the Navruz Nogais were complaining to the Don Cossack ataman about oppression by the Chemguy Circassians. They asked to migrate beyond the Don or to Astrakhan.
Kabardian–Kalmyk campaign (1738–1739)
In 1738, Kabardian rulers M. Kurgokin and Kara-Murza Aleev held back a large Nogai Horde. Kalmyks under Donduk-Ombo joined them. The allies marched on the Kuban and conquered Musa-Murza. A detachment of 800 Cossacks and 400 Kalmyks drove away 20,000 sheep.
In 1739, Aslanbech Qeytuqo and Donduk-Ombo captured 5,000 tents of the Bezlay Nogais and 2,000 tents of the Beybay Nogais.
Nogai raid on Abazinia (1747)
In January 1747, the Crimean Khan complained to the Ottoman government about the Kabardians. One of the complaints of the Crimeans was an accusation about them of killing the Nogai murza Khanmambet-Murza Bimurzina. However, as a result of the investigation, it was determined that Khanmambet Murza, together with an unidentified Crimean sultan, had carried out a raid against the lands of Abazins, a subject of the Kabardians. His aim was to steal horses and booty from the Abazins, however, the Abazins expelled the Nogai–Crimean allied forces and Khanmambet Bimurzina was mortally wounded during the incursion.
Raid on the Dzhanbuluk Nogais (1782)
In 1782, Circassian raiders attacked the Dzhanbuluk Nogais and drove off more than 1,600 horses. The Nogais failed to recover them.
The capture of Djaum-Adji
The Nogai leader Djaum-Adji, who was occasionally raiding the lands of Circassians was captured by the Circassians. He was forced to swear an oath to stop fighting the Circassians and to try to unite them with the Nogais.
Circassian–Nogai conflicts (1793–1839)
In October 1824, a mounted force of approximately 800 Circassians and rebel Kabardians, led by Jembulat Boletoqo, launched a raid from the Laba River basin into Kabardia. Near the village of Sabl, the raiders captured a herd of about 3,000 horses. Local Nogai tribesmen attempted to resist but were surrounded. A detachment of about 25 Cossacks under Esaul Popov rushed to assist but was also encircled near the Barsukly River. Despite fierce resistance, all Cossacks were killed. The raiders successfully withdrew to the mountains with the captured livestock. At least 897 Nogais fled Circassia between 1793 and 1839. The Circassians raided Nogai settlements, captured people, and sold them into slavery.
Aftermath
By the end of the 18th century, the Nogai Horde had fragmented. Many Nogais migrated to the Ottoman Empire or were absorbed into neighboring peoples. The Circassian–Nogai conflicts ended with the Russian conquest of the North Caucasus.
